questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a metadata repository actually store?
options: The underlying production data itself
The description of data — columns, owner, definition, lineage — separately from the data
Only backup copies of deleted tables
Network configuration settings for the database server
questions.explain: A metadata repository holds the description of a table (its structure, meaning, ownership, lineage), not the actual rows of data the table contains.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four common shapes a metadata repository takes, per this lesson?
options: Business glossary tools
Data dictionaries
Data catalogs
Customer relationship management (CRM) software
questions.explain: The four shapes covered are business glossary tools, data dictionaries, data catalogs, and purpose-built metadata registries — CRM software is a different category of tool entirely.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do organizations typically end up with more than one metadata repository?
options: Different teams adopt different tools at different times, for individually reasonable reasons
It is legally required to maintain at least three separate repositories
A single repository can only store metadata for one table at a time
Metadata repositories automatically duplicate themselves after one year
questions.explain: The BI team might pick a catalog bundled with their reporting tool, compliance maintains its own glossary — each choice makes sense locally, but together they create sprawl.

questions.q: What problem does this lesson say repository sprawl creates?
options: Metadata about the same table ends up in multiple places with nothing keeping them in sync
It makes the underlying production data run slower
It is impossible to have more than one glossary tool installed at once
It automatically deletes older metadata entries
questions.explain: When metadata about the same table lives in a glossary, a dictionary, and a separate catalog, those three descriptions can drift apart with nothing keeping them consistent.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why are data catalogs increasingly positioned as the 'single integration point'?
options: They pull business definitions, technical metadata, and lineage from other systems into one searchable place, rather than being yet another standalone repository
They are the only type of repository that can store technical metadata
They replace the need for a business glossary entirely
They are required by ISO/IEC 11179
questions.explain: Rather than compete with the glossary tool and dictionary as a fourth standalone repository, modern catalogs try to integrate and surface metadata from all of them in one searchable place.
